messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan Reyes had been with the police department for six years and had built his reputation as a calm, observant detective, the kind of man other officers trusted to walk into ugly situations without flinching. Outside work he lived in a quiet apartment with his wife, Marisol, in a North American suburb where the routines were ordinary enough to make what happened to him feel even more disorienting in hindsight. The violence had come not from a stranger on the street but from a romantic partner he had once trusted completely. During the last months of that relationship, an argument in their apartment escalated into him being shoved against a counter, held down, and struck hard enough to leave him with bruises and cuts; he could still picture the kitchen light, the cramped hallway, and the smell of stale alcohol on the other person’s breath as the fear turned physical. He had escaped, but he never felt that the danger ended with the door closing behind him.

Even now, certain moments would pull him straight back. If he felt nauseous after a long shift or after missing a meal, the sensation could open the door to a memory that arrived against his will, vivid and painfully detailed. He would suddenly know again the exact angle of the room, the pressure of a hand on his shoulder, the sound of slurred words, and sometimes he felt as if the voices from that night were playing inside his head with the same harsh clarity. The smell of alcohol was even worse; catching it on a suspect’s breath, in a bar hallway, or on a bottle at home would bring the whole scene flooding in before he had time to steady himself. Seeing visible injuries on others had the same effect, especially fresh wounds or bruising during an arrest or at a scene, because they seemed to confirm what he had come to believe about people: that they could become cruel without warning, that people were not what they seemed. Each of those moments also reinforced a deeper conclusion. Ethan had lost his faith in people, life, and any higher power he might once have believed was keeping order in the world, and he had begun to see himself as permanently outside everyone else’s easy trust, as if what had happened had marked him in a way that could not be undone.

The more those memories came, the more he tried to shut down anything that might let them in. He stopped relaxing after work because stillness felt dangerous to him; if he let himself sit on the couch too long, his mind would wander and the memory would force its way in. He learned to numb his feelings by staying busy, working late, reviewing case files, taking on extra tasks, anything that kept him from noticing the fear underneath. Physical contact became unbearable in a way he could not explain cleanly to Marisol at first. He avoided being touched even in ordinary moments, flinching from a hand on his back or tensing when she reached for him in bed, because contact felt too close to the old helplessness and made him fear he would not be able to control what surfaced next. Those efforts helped him get through the day, but they also kept him on guard in a body that never seemed to settle. He was always scanning for injuries on suspects, for the sour trace of alcohol, for the uneasy feeling of nausea that might signal another intrusive surge. The more he tried to outrun the memories, the more trapped he felt in a life organized around not being caught off balance.

Over time, the habits that were supposed to protect him began to deepen the very convictions he feared. Because he kept his emotions locked down and withdrew from touch, he felt increasingly separate from other people, as if connection belonged to everyone else and not to him. Avoiding relaxation left him alone with his thoughts at odd hours, and the quiet made him dwell on the idea that no one was fully safe to trust. Even at home he had trouble letting Marisol see how frightened he was, and the distance between them made his belief that he was an outsider feel more real. He hated what this had done to him, but he also could not shake the sense that the world had shown its true face and that it was only sensible to stay guarded. That guardedness did not keep the past away, however. In the field, the sights and smells he encountered kept setting off memories, and every time the images and voices returned he tightened his control even further. He became more vigilant with anything that resembled the original event, and ordinary life narrowed around his efforts to avoid being pulled under again.

By the time he came in for help, it was because the pattern was starting to cost him the parts of life he still cared about. He had noticed himself pulling away from Marisol, shrinking from her touch, and he was afraid she would eventually stop trying. He worried too that his work, which had once been the one place he could trust his competence, was becoming harder to manage because the same injuries and alcohol smells that turned up in his cases kept breaking open the memories. Ethan was not looking for a neat explanation so much as relief from the constant alertness and the sense that he had become cut off from ordinary human closeness. What he most feared was that the world really was as dangerous and false as it now seemed, and what he most hoped was that he might learn how to stay present with his wife and his life without every nausea, bruise, or whiff of alcohol dragging him back into that room.
